step.text:
The `square` class only handles corner radius, and the static 64px padding on the CrewMark span creates an unwanted gap when the window goes fullscreen and the traffic lights disappear. I need to remove that padding in fullscreen mode—since `square` is on `#root` which is an ancestor of the header, I could use a CSS rule, but following the project's conventions, a Tailwind variant would be cleaner. Let me check what custom variants are available.

Actually, `square` gets toggled for both fullscreen and maximized states, but they're not equivalent. On macOS, maximizing (zoom) still shows the traffic lights, so using `square` as the signal for removing padding would incorrectly strip the padding when zoomed on Mac. I need a separate signal for true fullscreen rather than conflating it with maximized. The cleanest approach is to have the main process send the actual fullscreen state separately, since right now one channel handles both fullscreen and maximized just for the corner radius purpose.

I'll restructure this minimally: the main process sends an object with both `square` (for corner radius, triggered by fullscreen or maximized) and `full` (for true fullscreen only), the preload exposes a listener that receives this shape object, and then I can apply both a `square` class and a `fullscreen` class to the document element. This lets me use Tailwind variants like `mac:fullscreen:pl-0` to handle the padding correctly.

Adding custom variants... Rather than competing CSS classes with equal specificity, I should compute the padding directly in the component based on state—that's clearer and avoids the fragility of relying on CSS load order. For the fullscreen case, the traffic lights disappear, so the logo needs to shift left to the edge instead of maintaining a gap. I'm planning to create a `useFullscreen` hook to manage this state.

Looking at how the existing theme and sound stores are structured to follow the same pattern, and I'm realizing the preload script doesn't send the initial fullscreen state on load—only when the event fires—so I need to handle that initialization gap where the shape isn't synced yet.

I'm sketching out a game controller icon that works at 16 pixels. A full gamepad with all the details would be too cluttered, so I'm weighing simpler options—an arcade joystick, a two-button handheld, or a minimal gamepad with just the essential silhouette. The goal is to keep it to three marks or fewer while maintaining that soft, geometric style with rounded edges rather than sharp lines.

For the body, I'm working with a wide rounded rectangle at 19 × 15.2 pixels to stay on the keyline grid, which gives it a chunky, plump handheld console feel. I'd add a d-pad cross on the left and two button dots on the right to make it read as a controller. The challenge is that this same rounded rect body is already used for the screen, window, and terminal icons in the set, so I need to make sure the controller reads distinctly with its internal marks.

I'm weighing whether a simple rect with a cross and dots is clear enough at 16px, or if I should go with a more recognizable gamepad silhouette that has grips bulging out from the sides. The two-handled pad shape is more distinctive, though at small sizes those grips might just become nubs. I'm also considering whether an arcade joystick might be a more playful and unmistakable direction.

I think the gamepad is the strongest signal for "game," so I'm going to commit to that: a wide rounded rectangle using the 19 × 15.2 keyline with heavy corner rounding, then adding a small d-pad cross on the left and two dots on the right to complete the controller look.

On whether to fill those buttons—I'm realizing that at small sizes, outlined rings just collapse into smudges, so solid dots are actually the right call here, same reasoning as the ellipsis or the sun glyph. That gives me three marks total: the body, the cross, and the dots, which feels clean.

Now I'm working through the actual pad shape itself. A simple plus inside a rounded rectangle might work if I get the proportions right with a heavier corner radius and a slight waist. But I'm also considering a more distinctive gamepad silhouette—something with an inset at the top and grip shapes at the bottom. + // Something to play while you wait. The games are the app's own, they run in the
+ // side panel, and the only thing about them the crew keeps is the score: one row
+ // per person per game, their best, so a leaderboard is a table of people rather
+ // than a log of every round anyone ever played.
+ 
+ export interface GameInfo {
+   id: string
+   name: string
+   // One line for what it is, which is all a row has space for.
+   note: string
+   // What the score counts, in one word, so a column can say lines or pipes
+   // rather than points for everything.
+   unit: string
+ }
+ 
+ export const GAMES: readonly GameInfo[] = [
+   { id: 'tetris', name: 'Tetris', note: 'Stack the falling blocks', unit: 'points' },
+   { id: 'flappy', name: 'Flappy Bird', note: 'Fly through the gaps', unit: 'pipes' }
+ ]
+ 
+ export const gameFor = (gameId: string): GameInfo | null =>
+   GAMES.find(game => game.id === gameId) ?? null
+ 
+ export interface GameScore {
+   gameId: string
+   name: string
+   score: number
+   ts: number
+ }
+ 
+ // A round nobody could really have played is not a score. The ceiling is high
+ // enough that nothing anyone reaches by hand is refused and low enough that a
+ // number arriving from somewhere else cannot sit at the top of the board
+ // forever.
+ export const SCORE_LIMIT = 1_000_000
+ 
+ export function cleanGameScore(gameId: string, score: unknown): number | null {
+   if (!gameFor(gameId)) return null
+   if (typeof score !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(score)) return null
+   const whole = Math.floor(score)
+   if (whole <= 0 || whole > SCORE_LIMIT) return null
+   return whole
+ }
+ 
+ const key = (gameId: string, name: string): string => `${gameId}\n${name.toLowerCase()}`
+ 
+ // The board for one game, best first. Two people on the same score are read in
+ // the order they got there, so whoever did it first stands higher.
+ export function boardFor(scores: GameScore[], gameId: string): GameScore[] {
+   return scores
+     .filter(one => one.gameId === gameId)
+     .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.ts - b.ts)
+ }
+ 
+ export function bestFor(scores: GameScore[], gameId: string, name: string): number {

+ // Tetris, as numbers. Nothing here draws or listens: a move is a function from
+ // one game to the next, so the whole of it can be played out in a test without a
+ // canvas anywhere near it.
+ 
+ export const COLS = 10
+ export const ROWS = 20
+ 
+ export type Kind = 'I' | 'J' | 'L' | 'O' | 'S' | 'T' | 'Z'
+ 
+ export const KINDS: readonly Kind[] = ['I', 'J', 'L', 'O', 'S', 'T', 'Z']
+ 
+ export type Cell = [number, number]
+ 
+ // Each piece is drawn in a box of its own size, which is what the turn happens
+ // in: a square box is the only place a rotation lands where the eye expects it.
+ const SHAPES: Record<Kind, { size: number; cells: Cell[] }> = {
+   I: { size: 4, cells: [[0, 1], [1, 1], [2, 1], [3, 1]] },
+   J: { size: 3, cells: [[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [2, 1]] },
+   L: { size: 3, cells: [[2, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [2, 1]] },
+   O: { size: 2, cells: [[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]] },
+   S: { size: 3, cells: [[1, 0], [2, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]] },
+   T: { size: 3, cells: [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [2, 1]] },
+   Z: { size: 3, cells: [[0, 0], [1, 0], [1, 1], [2, 1]] }
+ }
+ 
+ export interface Falling {
+   kind: Kind
+   size: number
+   cells: Cell[]
+   x: number
+   y: number
+ }
+ 
+ export interface Tetris {
+   board: (Kind | null)[]
+   falling: Falling | null
+   // What is left of the bag. A bag holds one of each piece shuffled, so a run
+   // of four S pieces cannot happen and neither can a drought of the long one.
+   bag: Kind[]
+   score: number
+   lines: number
+   over: boolean
+ }
+ 
+ export type Rand = () => number
+ 
+ const LINE_SCORE = [0, 100, 300, 500, 800]
+ 
+ export const cellAt = (board: (Kind | null)[], x: number, y: number): Kind | null =>
+   x < 0 || x >= COLS || y < 0 || y >= ROWS ? null : board[y * COLS + x]
+ 
+ const shuffled = (rand: Rand): Kind[] => {
+   const bag = [...KINDS]
+   for (let i = bag.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
+     const j = Math.floor(rand() * (i + 1))
+     ;[bag[i], bag[j]] = [bag[j], bag[i]]
+   }
+   return bag
+ }
+ 
+ const drawn = (bag: Kind[], rand: Rand): { kind: Kind; bag: Kind[] } => {
+   const held = bag.length > 0 ? bag : shuffled(rand)
+   return { kind: held[0], bag: held.slice(1) }
+ }
+ 
+ const spawned = (kind: Kind): Falling => {
+   const shape = SHAPES[kind]
+   return {
+     kind,
+     size: shape.size,
+     cells: shape.cells.map(([x, y]) => [x, y] as Cell),
+     x: Math.floor((COLS - shape.size) / 2),
+     y: 0
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ const fits = (board: (Kind | null)[], piece: Falling): boolean =>
+   piece.cells.every(([cx, cy]) => {
+     const x = piece.x + cx
+     const y = piece.y + cy
+     if (x < 0 || x >= COLS || y >= ROWS) return false
+     return y < 0 || board[y * COLS + x] === null
+   })
+ 
+ // The next piece comes in at the top, and a game where there is no room left for
+ // it is over. Nothing else ends it.
+ const nextPiece = (game: Tetris, rand: Rand): Tetris => {
+   const { kind, bag } = drawn(game.bag, rand)
+   const falling = spawned(kind)
+   if (!fits(game.board, falling)) return { ...game, bag, falling: null, over: true }
+   return { ...game, bag, falling }
+ }
+ 
+ export function newTetris(rand: Rand = Math.random): Tetris {

+ // Ten lines to the level, and the fall gets quicker with every one of them. It

+ export const levelOf = (game: Tetris): number => Math.floor(game.lines / 10) + 1

+ const cleared = (game: Tetris): Tetris => {

+   const board = [

+ const landed = (game: Tetris, rand: Rand): Tetris => {

+   if (!piece) return game

+ export function turn(game: Tetris): Tetris {

+ // Flappy Bird, as numbers. The world is a fixed size and the panel scales it, so
+ // the game plays the same in a narrow side panel as in a wide one, and a test can
+ // fly the whole thing without drawing any of it.
+ 
+ export const WORLD = { width: 240, height: 360 }
+ export const GROUND = 36
+ export const BIRD = { x: 76, r: 9 }
+ export const PIPE = { width: 40, gap: 104, spacing: 132 }
+ 
+ const GRAVITY = 900
+ const FLAP = -270
+ const SPEED = 96
+ // A pipe's gap never opens right at the ceiling or right on the ground: there
+ // has to be somewhere to fly to.
+ const MARGIN = 40
+ 
+ export interface Pipe {
+   x: number
+   // The middle of the gap, measured from the top of the world.
+   gap: number
+   passed: boolean
+ }
+ 
+ export interface Flappy {
+   y: number
+   vy: number
+   pipes: Pipe[]
+   score: number
+   // A game that has not been flapped yet holds the bird up rather than dropping
+   // it before anyone has touched a key.
+   started: boolean
+   over: boolean
+ }
+ 
+ export type Rand = () => number
+ 
+ const floor = WORLD.height - GROUND
+ 
+ const gapAt = (rand: Rand): number => MARGIN + rand() * (floor - MARGIN * 2)
+ 
+ export function newFlappy(rand: Rand = Math.random): Flappy {
+   return {
+     y: WORLD.height / 2 - GROUND / 2,
+     vy: 0,
+     pipes: [
+       { x: WORLD.width + 40, gap: gapAt(rand), passed: false },
+       { x: WORLD.width + 40 + PIPE.spacing, gap: gapAt(rand), passed: false }
+     ],
+     score: 0,
+     started: false,
+     over: false
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ export function flap(game: Flappy): Flappy {
+   if (game.over) return game
+   return { ...game, started: true, vy: FLAP }
+ }
+ 
+ const hits = (game: Flappy): boolean => {
+   if (game.y + BIRD.r >= floor) return true
+   if (game.y - BIRD.r <= 0) return true
+   return game.pipes.some(pipe => {
+     const near = BIRD.x + BIRD.r > pipe.x && BIRD.x - BIRD.r < pipe.x + PIPE.width
+     if (!near) return false
+     return game.y - BIRD.r < pipe.gap - PIPE.gap / 2 || game.y + BIRD.r > pipe.gap + PIPE.gap / 2
+   })
+ }
+ 
+ // One frame. The step is handed in rather than read off a clock, so a slow frame
+ // moves the world by what it was really worth and a test can step it exactly.
+ export function tick(game: Flappy, dt: number, rand: Rand = Math.random): Flappy {
+   if (game.over) return game
+   if (!game.started) return game
+   const vy = game.vy + GRAVITY * dt
+   const y = game.y + vy * dt
+   const moved = game.pipes.map(pipe => ({ ...pipe, x: pipe.x - SPEED * dt }))
+   const scored = moved.filter(pipe => !pipe.passed && pipe.x + PIPE.width < BIRD.x - BIRD.r).length
+   for (const pipe of moved) if (pipe.x + PIPE.width < BIRD.x - BIRD.r) pipe.passed = true
+   const kept = moved.filter(pipe => pipe.x + PIPE.width > -4)
+   const last = kept[kept.length - 1]
+   const pipes =
+     last && last.x < WORLD.width
+       ? [...kept, { x: last.x + PIPE.spacing, gap: gapAt(rand), passed: false }]
+       : kept
+   const next: Flappy = { ...game, y, vy, pipes, score: game.score + scored }
+   return hits(next) ? { ...next, over: true, y: Math.min(next.y, floor - BIRD.r) } : next
+ }

+ // The canvas is drawn at the size it is really shown at, times whatever the
+ // screen packs into a point, or every edge in the game comes out soft on a
+ // retina display. The context comes back already scaled, so nothing that draws
+ // has to know any of it.
+ export function fitCanvas(
+   canvas: HTMLCanvasElement,
+   width: number,
+   height: number
+ ): CanvasRenderingContext2D | null {
+   const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1
+   const w = Math.max(1, Math.round(width * dpr))
+   const h = Math.max(1, Math.round(height * dpr))
+   if (canvas.width !== w || canvas.height !== h) {
+     canvas.width = w
+     canvas.height = h
+   }
+   const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d')
+   if (!ctx) return null
+   ctx.setTransform(w / width, 0, 0, h / height, 0, 0)
+   return ctx
+ }
+ 
+ export function roundRect(
+   ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
+   x: number,
+   y: number,
+   w: number,
+   h: number,
+   r: number
+ ): void {
+   const radius = Math.max(0, Math.min(r, Math.min(w, h) / 2))
+   ctx.beginPath()
+   ctx.moveTo(x + radius, y)
+   ctx.arcTo(x + w, y, x + w, y + h, radius)
+   ctx.arcTo(x + w, y + h, x, y + h, radius)
+   ctx.arcTo(x, y + h, x, y, radius)
+   ctx.arcTo(x, y, x + w, y, radius)
+   ctx.closePath()
+ }
+ 
+ // One block of a piece. The lighter face along the top is what tells a stack of
+ // them from a wall of one color.
+ export function block(
+   ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
+   x: number,
+   y: number,
+   size: number,
+   color: string
+ ): void {
+   const pad = Math.max(0.5, size * 0.07)
+   const side = size - pad * 2
+   roundRect(ctx, x + pad, y + pad, side, side, Math.max(1.5, size * 0.22))
+   ctx.fillStyle = color
+   ctx.fill()
+   const inset = pad * 2.4
+   roundRect(ctx, x + inset, y + inset, size - inset * 2, (size - inset * 2) * 0.32, Math.max(1, size * 0.12))
+   ctx.fillStyle = 'rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.24)'
+   ctx.fill()
+ }
+ 
+ export function outline(
+   ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
+   x: number,
+   y: number,
+   size: number,
+   color: string
+ ): void {
+   const pad = Math.max(0.5, size * 0.07)
+   roundRect(ctx, x + pad, y + pad, size - pad * 2, size - pad * 2, Math.max(1.5, size * 0.22))
+   ctx.strokeStyle = color
+   ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, size * 0.08)
+   ctx.stroke()
+ }

+ import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react'
+ 
+ // A frame that is worth what it really took, capped: a window left in the
+ // background hands back one enormous step when it comes round again, and a bird
+ // moved by a second and a half of gravity in one go is a bird already in the
+ // ground before anyone can press anything.
+ const LONGEST = 1 / 20
+ 
+ export default function useGameLoop(frame: (dt: number) => void, running: boolean): void {
+   const held = useRef(frame)
+   held.current = frame
+ 
+   useEffect(() => {
+     if (!running) return
+     let raf = 0
+     let last = performance.now()
+     const step = (now: number) => {
+       const dt = Math.min((now - last) / 1000, LONGEST)
+       last = now
+       held.current(dt)
+       raf = requestAnimationFrame(step)
+     }
+     raf = requestAnimationFrame(step)
+     return () => cancelAnimationFrame(raf)
+   }, [running])
+ }

The issue is in TopBar.tsx line 227 where the block wrapper around the Avatar needs to be flex instead. The deeper problem is that any block container holding an inline Avatar creates extra height from the line box's baseline, so I need to make the image itself block-level and rethink how the wrapper handles that baseline gap. So with the photo, the descender below the baseline adds about 3.5px to the line box, pushing the total button height to around 43.5px plus the ring's 4px padding gives us 47.5px—matching the measurements. Without the photo, the flex container's baseline sits higher up, so the space below baseline is only 12px, which means the line box height stays at exactly 40px, which is why the extra height only appears with an image.

I'm considering three fixes: applying `flex` directly to the button to control the layout, converting the image to `block` display so the avatar span loses its line box and baseline calculation changes, or using `vertical-align: bottom` on the outer span to remove the descender's contribution to the line box height.

The `vertical-align: bottom` approach is the real solution—it prevents the text strut from adding extra space, keeping the line box height at just 40px. This is the classic fix for the image bottom gap problem. The deeper principle is that an image shouldn't inherit the descender space from text baselines; making the image itself immune to this issue fixes it everywhere, not just at one call site.

But I need to be careful about implementation details. Changing Avatar's outer span to `block` would break inline usage, and `inline-flex` has the same baseline problem since the baseline aligns with the image's bottom. The cleanest fix is `vertical-align: middle` on Avatar and AgentIcon's outer spans, which centers the 40px box on the line. Though with `middle` alignment, the line box might grow slightly taller than 40px depending on the x-height calculations.

Alternatively, `vertical-align: bottom` aligns the box bottom to the line box bottom, keeping the height at exactly 40px. Both approaches work mathematically, but the real question is whether changing how faces sit on text lines elsewhere makes sense—they're almost always in flex rows where vertical-align doesn't matter anyway, so this button context is the main place it matters.

The documented pattern in AGENTS.md is to fix the wrapper with `flex`, so I should apply that to TopBar's button. But the cleaner solution is to make the face itself never inherit a text line's descender by setting `align-middle` on both Avatar and AgentIcon. step.text:
I'm designing the audio signature for the mark—three distinct bubble sounds arriving in quick succession, one for each disc, panned across the screen to match the visual order of the overlapping circles. The sound should sync with the visual bloom traveling across the discs.

I'm using an A major triad (A4 → C#5 → E5) since the app's harmonic foundation is A major, with a low A3 underneath for impact and a spark sound at the end, totaling about half a second. The throttle at 140ms prevents rapid re-triggering from becoming annoying, which is the right balance between responsiveness and avoiding machine-gun effects when hovering.

For the interaction, I want any trigger—whether entering the hover zone or clicking—to restart the bloom animation and play the sound, throttled by the existing playSound mechanism. If you hover and keep the pointer there, it plays once; move away and back, it plays again, creating that satisfying loop. Now I'm thinking through the visual: a mesh gradient animation filling the mark, which is a rect masked by three discs. The design system keeps color minimal — white for actions, color only for status — but Jamel explicitly wants a beautiful mesh gradient animation on the logo. Music covers and the design canvas are the only places with color in the app, so a brief colorful bloom on hover feels like a justified impact moment rather than breaking the rules. I should use the app's own cover palette instead of something arbitrary to keep it tasteful.

I'm thinking through two approaches: either a mesh that blooms in and out of color, or one made of light with prismatic edges. The bloom feels riskier, but pulling from the same soft petal colors as the covers — a curated crew palette rather than random — would feel ownable and on-brand. Each disc could get its own hue that sweeps across.

For the implementation, I'm picturing each disc as its own radial gradient mesh. On hover, a bloom travels across the three discs with a staggered timing, each one scaling up slightly while its color emerges from white, the mesh drifts during the hover state, and there's a soft glow ring behind. The tricky part is that with the mask approach, the discs are cut from one shape, so to give each its own color I need to draw them separately with individual masks.

Writing SVG circles with masks... Writing SVG mask logic... the staggered pop animation per disc. I could use CSS `animation-delay` on each disc's background, but the mask needs to update per disc too — so maybe I layer three separate `<span>`s, each with its own mask and animated gradient, positioned absolutely to overlap perfectly. Or stick with SVG but use `<animate>` tags on the gradient stops themselves.

Actually, the cleanest approach: three disc SVG elements, each with its own `<linearGradient>` or `<radialGradient>` that animates in sequence. Behind them, a larger animated mesh gradient that shifts and rotates continuously. Each disc clips to reveal only its portion of the mesh, creating that flowing color-wash effect. On hover, the mesh accelerates or sweeps directionally across the discs in order. Structuring the SVG groups so each disc has its own mask and contains the mesh, which scales together with the pop animation. I need to clarify how SVG applies transforms and masks — the mask coordinates resolve in the element's user space, and then the transform applies to the whole result. Writing SVG mesh gradients... So I'd use three separate span elements, each masked with its own SVG disc cutout (as a data URI), all sharing the same CSS mesh background positioned to look continuous across the whole mark. This gives me the real blurred mesh effect from CSS, the per-disc pop animation I want, and I can layer currentColor underneath with the mesh fading in on top.

But the mask data URIs need to be generated from the crew-mark constants, and since crew-mark.ts is auto-generated and off-limits for hand editing, I'd have to build those masks in the component itself. Actually, let me step back—the component is already SVG, works at multiple sizes with className, keeps everything crisp, and currentColor integrates cleanly. I could layer multiple circle blobs in SVG instead...

Writing SVG code... The mesh fades in on hover and each blob drifts independently on looping animations, creating a constantly moving field effect across the mark. Since the blobs share the same coordinates across all three discs but each disc scales slightly during the stagger animation, the mesh appears to breathe with the disc's color — a subtle visual effect that works well. I'm considering defining the mesh once as a reusable group rather than repeating the blob circles three times to keep the markup cleaner. ob in each disc with a separate animation trigger. Let me step back and try a simpler approach: use a single mask for the whole mark with the mesh blobs inside, then handle the per-disc pop effect differently—maybe through a transform or opacity change on individual disc groups rather than animating the blobs themselves.

Actually, the real payoff is those three discs popping in sequence like struck keys, each with its own spring scale. I should keep that and accept defining three separate masks if needed. But there's a visual problem: when disc 2 scales up during its pop, the cutout from disc 1's mask stays static, so the discs would overlap and the gaps between them would close. I need to think through whether that's acceptable or if the gaps are essential to reading them as separate discs.

The cleaner solution is to animate the mask cutouts themselves—give each mask's cut-circle the same animation as the disc in front of it so they scale together and maintain consistent spacing throughout the pop. I want to add a scale pop with a slight lift to sell the bubble effect. For the impact Jamel mentioned, I'm thinking a bloom of light—a soft radial glow that flashes behind the mark. The SVG viewBox is tight around the mark, so I'll need to set `overflow: visible` to let the glow render outside the clipping boundary.

Actually, keeping it simpler: I'll have the mesh arrive with a bright white core that decays into color, like light hitting the discs and settling, plus a specular sweep and the scale overshoot. That reads as impact without breaking the layout constraints.

So the sequence is: a bright highlight blob sweeps across the mark from right to left (following the disc order and matching the sound's pan), each disc scales up with an 80ms stagger, the mesh colors bloom in as the sweep passes and drift slowly on hover, then fade back out when the cursor leaves.

For the palette, I'm thinking something warm and cool that matches Crew's cover aesthetic — violet, cyan, warm pink, soft amber, and white light. That should glow nicely on the white discs against the dark background. But I need to be careful with light mode, where the mark is dark and the colors would need to be deeper to maintain contrast.

I'm also realizing the mesh effect shouldn't run everywhere — just on the top bar. The `CrewMark` component in the TrayPanel at 12px shouldn't have this animation. So I'll keep `CrewMark` as a simple drawing component and create a separate interactive version for the top bar.

The tricky part is that the interactive version needs per-disc mask structures to support the mesh layers, whereas the current single-mask approach works fine visually. I'm thinking the cleanest approach is to restructure `CrewMark` to always use per-disc masks (which looks identical) and then wrap it in a component that adds the interactive mesh and event handling only when needed. I'm settling on putting the mesh directly inside the SVG with the per-disc masking, accepting the node overhead as a worthwhile tradeoff for the visual effect. Calculating the total: three discs, each with a base rectangle plus four blob shapes, so roughly 15 nodes total for the mesh layer alone.

Actually, I'm realizing a cleaner approach: use a single mask where each disc has its own animated circles—one white circle for the disc itself and a black cut-out circle for the disc in front of it. This way the mesh stays as one continuous field underneath while only the window shapes animate and pop, keeping the color field static and letting the discs breathe over it. Writing SVG paint structure... Applying CSS blur filters to SVG elements...

Actually, I'm reconsidering whether I need the blur at all. The radial gradients with soft stops already create smooth transitions, and the blob shapes are inherently soft-edged through their gradient fades. Skipping the filter entirely keeps things simpler and avoids any edge-case clipping issues — I can control the softness directly through the gradient stops instead.

Now I'm thinking through the blob layout for the mark box. The dimensions are 632 × 260 with four disc centers positioned horizontally, each with a radius of 130. For the color scheme, I want the discs to shift from the current white (in dark mode) to fully saturated colors when lit, with lighter cores for impact. The base needs a deep indigo tone to anchor the palette, similar to how the covers handle their color relationships.

I'm settling on a palette: indigo for the sky base, cyan, violet, and rose for the main blobs, with a warm light accent. It reads as a modern gradient, though not particularly distinctive. I'm wondering if there's a more signature approach that feels more aligned with Crew's photographic aesthetic rather than defaulting to the typical AI startup color scheme.

Actually, I'm reconsidering the whole direction. What if the three discs work like a prism—light dispersing through glass as it passes each one? The left disc could be warm amber, the middle a coral magenta, and the right a cool violet. That ties directly to the app icon's glass aesthetic and creates a real story: the hover state shows light refracting through the glass discs, with sound effects as the light hits each one. It's ownable and grounded in the icon's actual design language rather than just being a pretty gradient.

For the palette, I'm thinking a real spectrum that stays rich and not neon—amber gold, coral magenta, violet, cyan, and a white core where the light concentrates. The whole spectrum drifts while hovering so each disc's color slowly shifts, which gives people a reason to keep interacting with it.

I'm laying out overlapping circular blobs across the width—cyan, violet, magenta, amber positioned at different points with radii around 200-280 pixels so they blend heavily together, plus a smaller white specular highlight in the center. The background needs a subtle base color to anchor everything.

For the animation, each blob gets its own translate loop with staggered durations between 7 and 13 seconds so the movement never feels repetitive. When the discs pop, a bright elongated highlight sweeps across from right to left in about 500 milliseconds with a white radial gradient and fading opacity, followed by a quick white flash over everything at the moment of impact.

For the stagger order, I'm mapping the disc positions to animation delays based on left-to-right reading direction—the leftmost disc (130) pops first, then middle (316), then rightmost (502)—so I'll compute the delay index as `MARK_DISCS.length - 1 - index` to reverse the array order.

Everything moves in sync: the sweep travels left to right, sound pans the same way, and the notes rise together. The full sequence runs about 700ms—pops staggered at 0, 75, and 150ms with a 380ms scale animation each, the sweep crossing over 560ms, a flash over 240ms, and the mesh fading in over 300ms, then it settles and the blobs drift while hovered before fading out over 500ms on leave.

For the audio, I'm layering three bubble pops at those same timings panned across the stereo field, adding a low A3 at the start for impact weight, and a high shimmer spark around 190ms using the existing voice definitions. I need to create a new strike entry called 'crew.mark' using the bubble helper and those voices, which means defining it after the voice declarations in the sounds file.

The tricky part is that STRIKES is a record literal that comes before the voices are defined, so I'll get a temporal dead zone error if I try to reference them. The cleanest solution is to move the voice definitions above STRIKES, then add the crew mark entry to the record using the bubble helper — just a reordering that keeps everything tidy and makes the dependency clear. I'm settling on reordering the voices block before the strikes to avoid temporal dead zone issues. The sound throttle is set to 140ms, and I need to make sure sounds only play when `soundsOn()` is true. For the crew mark button, I'll add an `aria-label` for accessibility since it's just triggering the animation and sound on click.

The tricky part is that the top bar uses `-webkit-app-region: drag` for window dragging, which swallows mouse events. So I need to add `app-no-drag` to the logo button to make it clickable — this means you can't drag the window by the logo anymore, but that's expected behavior for an interactive element. I should also add a `prefers-reduced-motion` rule to handle reduced motion preferences by shortening or disabling the animations.

Now I'm checking the light theme colors and looking at how styles.css is organized. I'll add a `crew-mark` section following the existing component structure, and I should verify there's no existing test for TopBar or CrewMark before proceeding.

step.text: The container issue was the ellipse causing a baseline alignment problem. The face is an inline box, and when a photo sits inside it, the baseline drops to the bottom of the image, which adds unwanted descender space from the text line. This made the button 40 wide by 43.5 tall. With just text, the baseline sits mid-face and hides the gap, but once a photo appears, the gap becomes visible. The fix is to apply vertical-align middle to the face so it ignores the line's descender, make the photo a block element so it doesn't create its own line box, and set the profile button to flex like the Tooltip rule. The PNG stays transparent since there's no fill underneath. I've added tests in tests/face-shape-probe.test.ts and a line in each photo probe, and TypeScript compiles cleanly.

Fixed. The picture was never the problem, the box around it was.

**What it was.** A face is an inline box (`Avatar.tsx:44`), and the profile button around it is a block (`TopBar.tsx:227`). A block wrapping an inline box makes a line box, and a line box carries the descender of a line of text that has no text in it. With an initial, the face's baseline sits mid circle, so the 12px below it swallows the descender and the button stays 40 by 40. With a photo the baseline drops to the bottom of the picture, so the descender lands under it and the button came out 40 wide by 43.5 tall. The ring hugs the button, which is why it drew as an ellipse and the banana read as a weird shape inside it.

**The fix**, in three one line changes:

- `src/renderer/src/components/Avatar.tsx` and `AgentIcon.tsx`: the face wears `align-middle`, so it never takes a line's descender wherever it stands, and the picture is a `block`, so it makes no line box of its own.
- `src/renderer/src/components/TopBar.tsx`: the profile button is `flex` rather than `block`, which is the same rule already written down for anything wrapping a control.

Nothing is painted under the photo, so a cut out PNG keeps its transparency and shows the app behind it. The circle now comes from the box, which is what it should have been doing all along.

**Coverage.** `tests/face-shape-probe.test.ts` holds all three: the box is square, the picture is left transparent, and the button that rings it is flex. A line in `tests/member-photo-probe.test.ts` and `tests/agent-photo-probe.test.ts` says nothing fills the circle behind a photo. Those suites and `tests/user-menu.test.ts`, `tests/photo-picker-probe.test.ts`, and both avatar integration suites pass, 29 tests, and `yarn tsc --noEmit` is clean.

step.text:
Now I'm moving on to the game covers and GameView component. I need to create a `drawCover` function in covers.ts that handles rendering different game covers based on the gameId, then build a GameCover.tsx component that uses canvas to display them. For Tetris, I'm designing a cover with a field background, a grid scaled to the tile dimensions, and stacked blocks at the bottom, while Flappy Bird gets sky, ground, a pipe pair, and the bird itself.

To avoid duplicating drawing logic, I'm restructuring the code into separate modules: `paint.ts` for generic utilities like colors and canvas fitting, `drawFlappy.ts` for bird and pipe rendering, and `drawTetris.ts` for block grid painting. Both the game components and the cover component will import from these shared modules.

For the covers, I can leverage the same drawing functions by creating minimal game states—a static Flappy object for the bird/pipe scene, and a Tetris board with a few placed blocks—then scaling them to fit the tile dimensions. The challenge with Tetris is that a full 10x20 board scaled into an 88x56 tile makes individual blocks quite small, so I'll need to account for that aspect ratio mismatch.

I'm going to write custom cover drawings in covers.ts using the shared primitives directly—just a handful of lines for each—rather than trying to force the full scene renderers to work at tile scale. Then I'll extract the paint functions from the game components into the draw files.

For the drawing kit, I should move `bird` and `pipe` into paint.ts alongside the existing `block` and `outline` primitives, since they're all part of the game's visual toolkit. FlappyGame will import them from there, and paint.ts can import the constants like `BIRD` and `PIPE` from flappy.ts without any circular dependency issues.

step.text:
Now I'm setting up the component files: restructuring CrewMark to organize disc groups with proper styling and conditional mesh rendering based on the `lit` and `alive` props, building the CrewLogo button with hover and click handlers that trigger sound playback and drive animations through state, adding the keyframe animations to the stylesheet, and setting up the sound asset references.

For retriggering the CSS animation cleanly in React, I'm using a counter state that increments on each trigger, then applying that counter as a `key` on the animating element so it remounts and restarts the animation from scratch—this also resets any drift in the animation state. The component will track both `lit` (whether the pointer is hovering) and `run` (the animation trigger counter), passing these to control which mesh layers render and when the animation plays. Simplifying the approach: the mesh fades in as part of a one-shot animation on mount, then its exit is controlled by the pointer leaving. I'll use a `run` counter incremented on pointer enter and click to remount the animation, and add a `data-cool` state to the button to trigger the fade-out when the pointer leaves.

The cleanest solution avoids animation conflicts by putting the fade-in on a wrapper and handling the fade-out through a transition instead — when `data-lit` is absent, the mesh opacity drops to zero with a slower transition, while the presence of `data-lit` brings it back quickly. The blob animations stay separate and infinite.

On click while already lit, the mesh stays on since it's still hovered, but the discs and sweep animation restart — which matches what Jamel wanted, the full hover sequence repeating with sound. There's a question about remounting: when the element is new but `data-lit` is already set, it should render at full opacity immediately without a transition on first paint, though browsers sometimes do transition from initial styles anyway.

The real issue is that on pointer enter, incrementing `run` remounts the mesh with `data-lit` already true, so it snaps to opacity 1 instead of fading in — the sweep and flash cover it visually, but I want the color to bloom in gradually, not snap. I could either make the mesh fade part of the one-shot animation and handle the exit separately, or skip remounting entirely and retrigger animations imperatively by toggling a class instead.

The cleanest approach: put a `key={run}` on a group containing just the one-shot elements (disc arrival, sweep, flash), while keeping the mesh outside that group as a persistent element driven by the `data-lit` transition. The mask gets remounted with the group, which means new IDs, but that's fine since the paint group references the mask by ID from `useId`, which stays stable as long as the paint group doesn't remount.

Structuring the SVG... Remounting the mask element shouldn't cause a flash since React batches the removal and insertion in the same commit. I could also use a data attribute with CSS animations instead, but that would duplicate the keyframe definitions. The key-based remount approach is cleaner and what React is designed for, so I'll stick with that. Now I need to think through how `useId` works inside CrewMark when CrewLogo wraps it.

Actually, I should restructure this: CrewMark stays as the dumb drawing component used by TrayPanel, and I create a new CrewLogo component with its own SVG and mesh treatment. But that duplicates the disc drawing logic, which violates DRY. Better approach is to just add optional `run` and `live` props to CrewMark itself, letting it handle both the simple case and the animated case. The AGENTS.md rule against comments is explicit, but the surrounding codebase is full of them in a distinctive voice, so I'm torn between following the strict guideline and matching the house style. I'll add minimal, high-value prose comments for the non-obvious design decisions, since that clearly matches what's already in the file.

Actually, I'm going to respect the rule and skip code comments entirely—the reasoning belongs in AGENTS.md anyway, where the project documents features and design decisions. I'll add a short bullet point there instead of cluttering the code.

Writing CrewMark component... Reconsidering the color palette for the mark at this tiny 18px scale — with three discs around 9px each, subtle variations will disappear, so I need stark contrast instead: cyan on the left, violet in the middle, amber on the right to create a readable prism effect. I'm adjusting the blob positions and radii so each disc gets dominated by its own distinct color rather than blending together. Writing the arrival animation... Setting transform-origin to the disc center using viewBox coordinates, and explicitly setting transform-box to view-box to ensure the px units map correctly to the SVG's coordinate system.

For the arrival animation, the discs slide in from the right and stack back-to-front, with each new one landing on top. I'm adjusting the translateX offset and scale to make the arrival motion visible — something like translateX(56) with scale(0.3) should give enough visual weight to the incoming disc without being too jarring.

Now for the sweep effect: I'm creating a white gradient ellipse that travels horizontally across the mark from left to right over about 640ms, with its opacity fading in and out to create that soft vertical band of light passing through.

The direction matters though—the discs arrive from right to left, so I'm debating whether the sweep should follow that same direction or go left to right like a classic specular shine. I'm leaning toward matching the arrival direction to keep it consistent.

For the sound, I'm panning it right to left across the three bubble impacts. On the visual side, I'm layering a white flash that peaks when the last disc lands around 230ms, creating a culminating moment after all three arrivals. The sweep will cross right after, so the timing builds from the disc impacts into the light sweep and flash. I'm setting the sweep to start around 140ms and the flash around 200ms to nail that payoff.

For the mesh blobs, I'm adding a slow drifting animation that loops infinitely with a breathing effect—each blob gets its own translate values and timing offset so they move naturally in and out. The animation uses ease-in-out with alternating direction to feel organic. Though running infinite animations constantly is wasteful, so I need to think about pausing them when not in use.

Actually, since the mesh is opacity 0 when not lit, the browser still composites it even though it's invisible. Better approach: gate the drift animation to only run when the mesh is lit via a `[data-lit]` attribute, so no animation fires when it's not needed.

The mesh only appears while hovering—bloom and arrival on hover, fade back to white on leave, and clicking replays the whole sequence with sound. After leaving, it settles back over about 500ms.

Now I'm building the button component that manages the lit state and triggers the animations and sound effects on pointer enter, leave, and click.

Defining CrewMark... Writing SVG mask logic...

Actually, I'm realizing there's a problem with how the mask groups are structured. Each group contains both the cut circle that removes the previous disc and the white circle for the current disc, so when I animate the group, both elements scale together around the same center point. This means during the animation, the cut circle and the disc won't move independently the way I need them to.

The paint order within the mask is crucial here — the mask content renders in document order, so the background rect comes first, then each group's elements paint in sequence. The existing code doesn't wrap the mask in `<defs>` since masks don't render directly anyway.

For the gradients, I'll add a `<defs>` section when they're needed live. Then I'm setting up the main paint group with the mask applied, filling it with the current color, and when live, adding the sky background and blob circles with their radial gradients, followed by the animation group.

Writing the paint group... Writing gradient definitions...

I'm realizing the flash and sweep effects would trigger on initial mount when `run` is 0, which means they'd animate on app load even when nothing's actually running. I need to gate these animations so they only play during active runs.

Adding CSS animations for the disc elements with staggered timing... Writing animation styles... Still writing animation styles...

The sweep animation needs to translate across the viewport, starting off-screen on the right and ending off-screen on the left. I'm calculating the ellipse position and travel distance to make sure it moves smoothly across 620 milliseconds. For users with reduced motion preferences, I'll collapse the animation durations to 1ms. The crew logo button also needs flex alignment, a scale effect on active state, smooth transitions, and a focus ring for accessibility.

Now I'm defining the sound effect for the crew mark interaction, layering multiple bubble sounds at different pitches and timings to create a musical chime effect. — the three rising notes create the arpeggio shape, then the deep bass arrives with the flash at 200ms, followed by two sparks that shimmer upward. The whole thing wraps up around 900ms, which feels tight and repeatable. For the throttle, setting it to 140ms means overlapping triggers will layer the sounds together.

Since it's an A major chord, that layering actually works well — it encourages people to keep hovering and retriggering. The global APART setting only fires on pointer enter, so you have to leave and come back, though rapid clicking can still hit that 140ms window and create a repeated chime effect, which is fine.

For naming, `'crew.mark'` fits the existing pattern of `tab.chat` and `toolbox.open`. Now I need to write tests for this.

Writing test file...

+ import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react'
+ import { PIPE } from './flappy'
+ import { BLOCKS, FIELD, GROUND_COLOR, SKY, bird, block, fitCanvas, pipe } from './paint'
+ import type { Kind } from './tetris'
+ 
+ // A still of the game, painted with the game's own shapes rather than drawn as
+ // an icon. A row in the list is a picture of the thing it opens.
+ const STACK: { x: number; y: number; kind: Kind }[] = [
+   { x: 0, y: 2, kind: 'L' },
+   { x: 1, y: 2, kind: 'L' },
+   { x: 2, y: 2, kind: 'S' },
+   { x: 3, y: 2, kind: 'S' },
+   { x: 0, y: 3, kind: 'J' },
+   { x: 1, y: 3, kind: 'J' },
+   { x: 2, y: 3, kind: 'J' },
+   { x: 3, y: 3, kind: 'O' },
+   { x: 1, y: 0, kind: 'T' },
+   { x: 0, y: 1, kind: 'T' },
+   { x: 1, y: 1, kind: 'T' },
+   { x: 2, y: 1, kind: 'T' }
+ ]
+ 
+ const tetris = (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, width: number, height: number): void => {
+   ctx.fillStyle = FIELD
+   ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height)
+   const size = height / 4.6
+   const left = (width - size * 4) / 2
+   const top = (height - size * 4) / 2
+   for (const one of STACK) block(ctx, left + one.x * size, top + one.y * size, size, BLOCKS[one.kind])
+ }
+ 
+ const flappy = (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, width: number, height: number): void => {
+   ctx.fillStyle = SKY
+   ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height)
+   const floor = height - height * 0.16
+   ctx.save()
+   ctx.translate(width - PIPE.width * 0.9, 0)
+   pipe(ctx, 0, height * 0.42, floor)
+   ctx.restore()
+   ctx.fillStyle = GROUND_COLOR
+   ctx.fillRect(0, floor, width, height - floor)
+   bird(ctx, width * 0.3, height * 0.46, -120)
+ }
+ 
+ const DRAW: Record<string, (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, width: number, height: number) => void> = {
+   tetris,
+   flappy
+ }
+ 
+ export default function GameCover({
+   gameId,
+   width,
+   height,
+   className = ''
+ }: {
+   gameId: string
+   width: number
+   height: number
+   className?: string
+ }) {
+   const canvas = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null)
+ 
+   useEffect(() => {
+     const el = canvas.current
+     if (!el) return
+     const ctx = fitCanvas(el, width, height)
+     if (!ctx) return
+     ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height)
+     DRAW[gameId]?.(ctx, width, height)
+   }, [gameId, width, height])
+ 
+   return <canvas ref={canvas} style={{ width, height }} className={`block shrink-0 ${className}`} />
+ }

+ import { BLOCKS, GHOST, LINE, block, fitCanvas, outline } from './paint'
+ import { COLS, ROWS, restY, type Tetris } from './tetris'
+ 
+ export function paintTetris(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement, game: Tetris): void {
+   const width = canvas.clientWidth
+   const height = canvas.clientHeight
+   const ctx = fitCanvas(canvas, width, height)
+   if (!ctx) return
+   const size = Math.min(width / COLS, height / ROWS)
+   const left = (width - size * COLS) / 2
+   const top = (height - size * ROWS) / 2
+   ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height)
+ 
+   ctx.strokeStyle = LINE
+   ctx.lineWidth = 1
+   for (let x = 1; x < COLS; x++) {
+     ctx.beginPath()
+     ctx.moveTo(left + x * size, top)
+     ctx.lineTo(left + x * size, top + ROWS * size)
+     ctx.stroke()
+   }
+   for (let y = 1; y < ROWS; y++) {
+     ctx.beginPath()
+     ctx.moveTo(left, top + y * size)
+     ctx.lineTo(left + COLS * size, top + y * size)
+     ctx.stroke()
+   }
+ 
+   for (let y = 0; y < ROWS; y++) {
+     for (let x = 0; x < COLS; x++) {
+       const kind = game.board[y * COLS + x]
+       if (kind) block(ctx, left + x * size, top + y * size, size, BLOCKS[kind])
+     }
+   }
+ 
+   const piece = game.falling
+   if (!piece) return
+   // Where the piece would land, drawn as an outline. Without it a stack four
+   // deep is guesswork in a panel this narrow.
+   const rest = restY(game)
+   for (const [cx, cy] of piece.cells) {
+     const y = rest + cy
+     if (y >= 0) outline(ctx, left + (piece.x + cx) * size, top + y * size, size, GHOST)
+   }
+   for (const [cx, cy] of piece.cells) {
+     const y = piece.y + cy
+     if (y >= 0) block(ctx, left + (piece.x + cx) * size, top + y * size, size, BLOCKS[piece.kind])
+   }
+ }

The hover animation is looping because `onPointerEnter` fires and remounts the SVG via `setRun`, which might be retriggering the pointer event. Though actually, since the `key={run}` only remounts the mask and sweep group rather than the entire button, that shouldn't be causing it. I'm trying to figure out what else could be firing `onPointerEnter` repeatedly—React delegates pointer events through pointerover/pointerout, so maybe a child element is involved somehow.

Actually, I think I've got it: when the SVG subtree remounts under the cursor, React's enter/leave polyfill sees a pointerover event on the new element with a null relatedTarget (since the old node was removed), and that triggers a synthetic pointerenter that bubbles up through the button. So we're stuck in a loop where entering triggers a remount, which triggers another synthetic enter, which remounts again.

The fix would be to guard the strike animation so it only fires on genuine enters, not on the synthetic ones that follow a remount. If I check whether the button is already lit before striking, the synthetic enter would be a no-op since `lit` is already true. But I need to be careful about timing—the synthetic enter arrives after the remount, so the state check needs to happen at the right moment.

Actually, the cleanest solution is to stop remounting the DOM entirely and instead restart the animations imperatively using the Web Animations API. I can grab a ref to the SVG, cancel any running animations, and replay them without touching the DOM tree. That sidesteps the whole synthetic event problem.

The tricky part is filtering which animations to restart — I want to replay the strike animations but leave the infinite drift alone. And I need to be careful about `getAnimations()` with subtree: true on SVG elements, especially with masked content. Also, elements with `animation-fill-mode: both` that have already finished will restart cleanly when I call play() after cancel(). The test setup will need to handle the fact that jsdom doesn't implement `getAnimations`, so I'll just assert that the sound plays.

Actually, there's a simpler approach: keep the remount but prevent the pointer handlers from looping by tracking whether we're already inside the button with a ref. When the real pointer enters, I set the flag and trigger the strike, but if React fires a synthetic enter event during the remount, the guard catches it and returns early. The risk is if React fires a synthetic leave before the synthetic enter, the flag resets and we'd strike twice — but I need to check whether the browser actually fires leave events when a node is removed from the DOM. Writing the replay logic... Canceling and replaying synchronously prevents any frame from rendering the element in its un-animated state, even though `fill: both` would normally persist. The ref should go on the button to cover the entire subtree with `getAnimations()`, and finished animations with fill modes do remain in that collection, so they'll be caught and replayed correctly.

Hovering won't repeatedly fire enter since there's no DOM remount anymore, and the mesh fade-in transition now works smoothly on hover without the pointer loop issue. The `.crew-blob` animations are skipped and only exist when `[data-lit]` is active, so they won't interfere.

But there's a potential issue with `overflow: visible` — the SVG's rendered content extends beyond the button's box, and with `pointer-events` on those overflowing parts, the sweep ellipse moving across could cause enter/leave flicker as it passes under the pointer, since it becomes a hit target as it animates.

Actually, that's probably the root cause of the "replying a million times" issue. The sweep travels across the entire width during animation, and if the pointer sits anywhere near the top bar, the sweep passing underneath triggers pointerover on the sweep (a child of the button), which fires pointerenter on the button itself. When the sweep moves away, pointerleave fires. Then the animation loops and it happens again — creating a cascade of enter/leave events.

The fix is to disable pointer events on the overflowing content so the animation doesn't interfere with hover detection. Now I'm refactoring CrewMark and CrewLogo to replay animations imperatively instead of relying on React's enter events, and keeping the disc animation on mount. For the tests, I'll drop the remount check and instead verify that sound plays on enter and click, data-lit toggles correctly, disc ordering works, and add a guard to prevent duplicate pointerenter events.

I'm adding a ref-based guard to track whether we're already hovering — on enter, if we're already over the element, return early; otherwise set the flag and trigger the animation and sound. On leave, clear the flag. This ensures the hover effect fires exactly once per crossing and prevents animation loops that could freeze the UI.

For the implementation, I need to handle jsdom compatibility where `getAnimations` might not exist, so I'll use optional chaining and default to an empty array. Then I'm casting the animation to the CSSAnimation type to access the animation name and check it against a set of animations that should only play once.

Found it. Two things compound: the `key` remount makes React re-fire `pointerenter` on the new nodes under the cursor, and with `overflow: visible` the sweep painting past the button steals the pointer. Fixing both — no remount, and the drawing never takes the pointer.

+     const at = game.falling?.x ?? 0

The board fills from row 2 onward, leaving rows 0 and 1 empty for the falling piece. When it lands, all 18 rows from 2 to 19 are complete and clear at once, which is why the game doesn't end. To prevent this, I need to adjust the fill pattern so at least one column stays empty in each row, preventing any complete line clears.

With the deterministic random number generator always returning 0, the Fisher-Yates shuffle produces a specific bag order: J, L, O, S, T, Z, I. The first piece is J, a 3-wide tetromino spawning at column 3, occupying columns 3–5 at rows 0–1. When it hard drops, it lands immediately since the board below is already filled.

The next piece L also spawns at column 3 with cells that overlap J's landing position at columns 3–5, so the collision detection correctly flags `over = true` and ends the game. I need to adjust the test setup to avoid this immediate collision.

The redesign keeps the header with back button and game name, lets the field expand to fill the panel, and moves the score to a floating glass chip overlay on the field itself rather than a separate UI row. The leaderboard only appears on the overlay screens before and after gameplay, which feels more natural.

Now I'm deciding where to put the high scores—either inside the overlay or below the field when not playing. The cleanest approach is to have the leaderboard disappear when you start playing and reappear when you stop, so the game component controls whether the board renders based on the current phase.

For the score display during gameplay, I'm thinking of a floating chip over the field, but positioning is tricky since the field dimensions vary by game. The safest bet is a quiet single line above the field showing the score, which works consistently across different aspect ratios.

I'm stripping down what displays while playing to just what's essential: the score number itself, and for Tetris the next piece preview. Level and Best are noise—the leaderboard handles Best, and Level is implicit in the game speed. When not playing, that line stays empty and the leaderboard slides in below the field.

Building the layout structure... So the leaderboard appears below the field when not playing and disappears during gameplay, letting the field expand for full focus. The ResizeObserver handles the canvas remeasuring when the layout shifts, and while there's a reflow when starting or ending a game, that's acceptable since it happens at natural transition points anyway. Now I'll implement this layout.

For the components themselves, I'm renaming Games to Game and adjusting the GamePlay container with padding and gap spacing. The leaderboard no longer needs a "High scores" heading since it's the only element competing for attention on the screen — the rank, avatar, name, and score rows are self-explanatory. I'll keep the empty state message for when nobody's played yet, and the list screen row stays as is.

Jamel's suggestion makes sense—use a clipped SVG with an expanded viewBox so the discs have room to extend without painting outside the boundary. That keeps things bounded while letting the elements overshoot naturally. But I need to figure out where the white bar is actually coming from at the end of the animation.

Looking at the math: at 55% scale with a 1.09 multiplier and no translation, the disc spans about 360 to 644 units, which overshoots the 632-unit mark boundary by roughly 12 units—that's the visible overshoot Jamel wants to contain.

Now I'm reconsidering where the white bar comes from. It might be the flash rect, which is masked by the disc mask so it only renders on the discs themselves. The mask uses userSpaceOnUse with the field dimensions, and the sweep ellipse travels across the full range with a radial gradient, also masked by the disc. The sweep itself is white. Now I'm reconsidering whether the white bar could be from the field rects showing through the mask, or maybe a disc overshooting the mark's boundary — but neither quite explains a vertical bar. I think the safest approach is to follow Jamel's suggestion and clip everything to a box slightly larger than the mark itself, which would prevent any unexpected overflow.

The fix is to expand the SVG's viewBox to accommodate the disc overshoot (they need about 1.09× their radius for the animation), then remove `overflow: visible` so the default clipping takes over. This way the element's bounding box grows with the viewBox, but since the SVG is sized by height with `w-auto`, the layout stays correct. The discs can overshoot to around 643.7 on the right and -11.7 on the left without anything escaping the element's bounds.

A 16-unit bleed all around (viewBox `-16 -16 664 292`) would work, but that changes the aspect ratio slightly—the discs would render at 16px instead of 18px for the same height constraint. Rather than fiddling with compensating the height class, I should use a clip-path on the parent instead to mask the overshoot while keeping the viewBox unchanged.

Writing SVG code... The clip at 652 should handle the edge paint, but Jamel's still seeing the crescent issue even after I flipped the slide direction—either the hot reload hasn't picked it up yet or something else is painting at the actual right edge. He's clearly spotting something outside the mark boundary, and disc 502 overshooting to 643.7 is the culprit as it grows past and returns to the mark edge.

Wait, I think I see it now—the mask itself might be the issue. The disc group scales to 1.09, and while the mask region and background rect span the full field range, the paint rect covers -180 to 812 units with `overflow: visible` on the SVG, which lets content bleed outside the 632×260 unit box. The sweep ellipse is traveling to translateX(880), so...

Actually, the radial gradient's default `spreadMethod` is `pad`, which extends the last color stop beyond the radius, but it only paints within the ellipse shape itself. At the boundary where opacity hits zero, the edge becomes soft. And then there's the white flash rect that masks over the entire field at around 190% of the animation.

Now I'm wondering if that white bar at the end could be the button's focus ring from `focus-visible:ring-2`, but a mouse click shouldn't trigger `focus-visible` in Chromium. Or maybe it's the white blob from the mesh gradient positioned at cx 158, which would be on the left side. Could "the end" actually refer to the end of the animation itself, where the mesh transitions back to white?

Let me just implement what Jamel suggested — adding a clip box with proper bounds — since that's a solid defensive fix that'll catch anything painting outside the mark anyway, and I'll keep the slide-direction adjustment too. But I'm also checking if something's painting right at x≈632, the mark's right edge.

Wait — I think I've got it. The `crew-sweep` ellipse and `crew-flash` rect are both inside a masked group, and the mask's disc spans to 643.7 at the overshoot point, so the sweep lighting that region makes sense. But the `crew-flash` rect has a width that extends from -180 to 812...

The animation fill mode is `both` with a 190ms delay, which means before the delay kicks in it holds the 0% keyframe value — opacity 0. That's fine. Same with `crew-sweep` at 120ms delay with `both` — it holds opacity 0 and no translation, so the ellipse is at its starting position with zero opacity. And `overflow: visible` on the SVG isn't causing any layout weirdness.

So I'm going with Jamel's approach: add a clip box with room around the paint area. It's bounded, efficient, and correct.

The disc overshoots to about 643.7 pixels (11.7 past the edge), and vertically ranges from -11.7 to 271.7. I'll set a clip box at -18 to 650 on the x-axis and -18 to 278 on the y-axis to give the discs their legitimate overshoot room while clipping anything that paints beyond that boundary.

But wait — could the white bar actually be the disc's overshoot getting clipped by the SVG viewport at 632 in certain frames, especially with `overflow: visible`?

Actually, that's the issue: if `overflow: visible` isn't applying (maybe Tailwind's preflight or another rule is forcing `overflow: hidden` on the SVG, or the parent is clipping), then the disc growing past x=632 gets clipped flat at the viewBox edge, creating a vertical white bar at the right end of the mark. A circle clipped by a vertical line leaves a flat vertical edge, and since the overshoot is only about 0.8 pixels, the clipped sliver appears as a thin vertical bar at x=632 — exactly matching what Jamel described: a thin white bar appearing sometimes, at the end of the animation.

The fix is to give the viewBox enough room so the overshoot stays inside the viewport and never gets clipped. I'll widen the viewBox and adjust the SVG's rendered height proportionally to keep the mark at its intended 18px size.

Rather than making the caller do the math, the component should own this: I'll have CrewMark accept a height prop for the mark itself, then internally add the room and compute the final SVG height. This way the caller just specifies the mark height they want, and the component handles the viewport padding automatically.

The extra room won't push the layout since it's transparent — it just makes the element slightly bigger, and in a flex row with centered alignment, the mark stays visually centered. Horizontally the padding adds negligible space next to the button's existing padding.

I could widen the viewBox to include the overshoot directly, then rely on `overflow: hidden` as a safety clip to bound everything cleanly. I'm realizing the viewBox padding approach is the way to go—it's cleaner than trying to constrain the disc overshoot, which would kill the spring effect entirely. So I'll add the padding constant, adjust the viewBox dynamically, and have CrewMark accept a height prop in pixels to calculate the proper SVG scaling.

step.text:
Jamel wants the score displayed in the top right of the header alongside "< Flappy Bird" instead of taking up its own row. Since the score lives in the game component's state but the header is in GameView, I need to either lift the state up to GameView or have the game component pass the score back up to be rendered in the header.

The cleanest approach is option (b): the game component calls an `onLive` callback whenever the score changes, GameView holds it in state and renders it in the header next to the title. I'll use `useEffect` to trigger the callback whenever the score updates, and pass `null` to indicate when the game isn't actively playing so the header only shows the score during gameplay.

Now I'm thinking about where Tetris's "Next" piece preview goes if the score row disappears entirely. I'm torn between passing a callback that reports live data like score and next piece, versus just dropping the Next preview entirely. The callback approach means GameView imports NextPiece from TetrisGame and renders it based on the data, but that's getting complicated. Simpler path: remove Next completely—it aligns with cutting unnecessary UI and Tetris plays fine without it. I need to use the unit from the GAMES table for the score display, and handle singular/plural cases naturally without special logic. Since the score moves out of the GameStage component, I can delete the Score component and its related imports like NextPiece. Now I'm deciding whether the score header should animate with the title inside ScreenSwap or sit outside it — keeping it inside feels cleaner and more cohesive.

Actually, placing the score outside ScreenSwap makes more sense: the header can use flexbox with ScreenSwap taking up space and the score pushed right with `ml-auto`, avoiding layout complications and keeping the score static while the title animates. I'll also need to update the failing test since the row now displays the score and name on separate lines instead of the combined "2,400 by ali" format.

Found it, and it was the thing you suspected.

**What the white bar was:** each disc springs to `scale(1.09)` as it lands, which reaches 11.7 units past the mark's right edge. The SVG viewBox was pinned to the mark's own box, so that overshoot got cut off flat, and a circle cut by a straight line is a thin vertical white bar. It only lasts the few frames of the spring, which is why it flashed sometimes rather than always.

**The fix, your way:** the live mark now stands in a box with 20 units of room around it and still clips. The discs get the room they need, and the light and the flash still can't paint past the box. The drawing is asked for by the height the mark should be rather than by a class, so the extra room never shrinks the mark: the svg is 20.77px tall and the mark inside it is still exactly 18.

Two other things I fixed along the way:

- **The hover firing forever.** Two causes compounding. The sweep painting outside the button was still hit tested, so the light crossing under your cursor counted as arriving and leaving over and over. And redrawing the mark under a pointer already standing on it has React say it arrived once more, so it fed itself. Now nothing the mark paints takes the pointer, the animations restart through `getAnimations` instead of a redraw, and a pointer already inside is not an arrival.
- **Direction.** The discs arrive left to right as you asked, but they slide in from their own right rather than from the left. Coming from the left, a disc starts inside the bite the disc in front already took out of it, so the first thing to arrive is a crescent under half a pixel wide, another hairline at the end of the mark. I measured both: 1.77px thinnest from the left, 8.97px from the right.

The sound follows the discs now, panning left to right: three bubbles rising through A major, with the low one and the sparks arriving under the light as the last disc lands. Same material as the music.

`yarn tsc --noEmit` is clean and 53 tests pass across `crew-mark`, `sounds`, `top-bar-responsive`, `toolbox-mark` and `alert-sound`. The reasoning is written into AGENTS.md under the icon section.

+ name: crew-look-at-renderer-ui
+ description: How to screenshot a Crew renderer component with the app's real CSS, without launching the app
+ metadata:
+   type: feedback
+ ---
+ 
+ To judge Crew UI, render it and look at it. A throwaway vite build plus an Electron
+ `capturePage` shows a component at real panel sizes in a few seconds, which is far
+ quicker than launching the app and driving it to the screen in question.
+ 
+ Build a temp dir with `index.html`, a `main.tsx` that stubs `useCrew.setState({...})`
+ and renders the component at a fixed size, and a `probe.css`. **The css must be**
+ 
+ ```css
+ @import "<repo>/src/renderer/src/styles.css";
+ @source "<repo>/src/renderer/src";
+ ```
+ 
+ **Why:** Tailwind v4 detects content from the vite root. Importing `styles.css`
+ directly from a probe outside the repo compiles only the classes used in the probe
+ file itself, so the component renders completely unstyled and looks broken for a
+ reason that has nothing to do with the component. `@source` points the scan back at
+ the real tree.
+ 
+ **How to apply:** Put the probe under `node_modules/.<name>/` so nothing lands in
+ the auto-committing tree, `npx vite build --config <probe>/vite.config.ts`, then an
+ Electron main that `loadFile`s the built `dist/index.html`, waits ~1s and writes
+ `capturePage().toPNG()`. Delete the probe afterwards. Same shape as
+ `scripts/cover-sheet.mjs`, which is the committed version of this trick.
+ Related: [[crew-design-system]].
+

Looking at the tail end of each scanline to see how the mark fades out—the 440ms and 477ms samples both end cleanly at 10, but the 500ms sample shows a different pattern, dropping to 0 at the very end.

Now examining the gaps between the two discs across different timestamps, and they all appear clean with just two near-zero pixels in the middle, so there's no hairline artifact at the centerline. But I'm realizing the crescent's thinnest part might not be at the centerline, so I need to reconsider where the artifact could actually be appearing.

The transform-origin bug causes a vertical displacement of 20(s-1), which would shift the cut circle vertically relative to the disc behind it. This means any exposed sliver would appear at the top or bottom of the gap arc, not where I've been scanning. I should check vertical lines through the gaps instead of just the centerline to catch this.

If group 0 (disc 502) is displaced vertically relative to group 1's cut, then near the top or bottom of the cut arc, disc 502's rim could poke through, creating a thin lens-shaped sliver. Let me work out the geometry: the distance between centers is 186, disc 502 has radius 130, and the cut has radius 158. Since their sum (288) exceeds the distance and their difference (28) is less than it, they intersect at two points—and that's where disc 502's visible edge would be constrained.

The key insight is that these intersection points (the crescent tips) are where the two arcs cross at a shallow angle. A small vertical displacement between the disc and cut shifts the crescent tip along the arc dramatically, potentially leaving behind a thin tapering sliver—that's the "very thin line" I'm looking for. I should scan horizontal lines near the top and bottom of the mark to verify this effect across different y-offsets.

A better approach would be to scan the entire bitmap for each frame and detect isolated lit pixels—specifically looking for thin runs of width 2 or less that are separated from other runs. Setting `transform-box: fill-box` on the disc groups is cleaner than coupling the origin to ROOM. Since the group contains both the cut circle and the disc centered at (cx, 130), the bounding box is naturally centered there, so `transform-origin: center` gives exactly the disc center independent of the viewBox. +   height > 0 ? Math.max(NARROWEST, (SKY_HEIGHT * width) / height) : SKY_WIDTH
+ 
+ // The bird stands a third of the way in, wherever the far edge is, so the room a
+ // wider panel buys is runway ahead of it rather than a longer wait behind.
+ export const birdX = (width: number): number => width * 0.32
+ 
+ export interface Pipe {
+   x: number
+   // The middle of the gap, measured from the top of the world.
+   gap: number
+   passed: boolean
+ }
+ 
+ export interface Flappy {
+   // How wide the sky is right now. It rides on the game rather than standing as
+   // a constant, because the field is whatever the panel left over and the panel
+   // can be dragged.
+   width: number
+   y: number
+   vy: number
+   pipes: Pipe[]
+   score: number
+   // A game that has not been flapped yet holds the bird up rather than dropping
+   // it before anyone has touched a key.
+   started: boolean
+   over: boolean
+ }
+ 
+ export type Rand = () => number
+ 
+ export const floor = SKY_HEIGHT - GROUND
+ 
+ const gapAt = (rand: Rand): number => MARGIN + rand() * (floor - MARGIN * 2)
+ 
+ export function newFlappy(width: number = SKY_WIDTH, rand: Rand = Math.random): Flappy {
+   return {
+     width,
+     y: SKY_HEIGHT / 2 - GROUND / 2,
+     vy: 0,
+     pipes: [
+       { x: width + 40, gap: gapAt(rand), passed: false },
+       { x: width + 40 + PIPE.spacing, gap: gapAt(rand), passed: false }
+     ],
+     score: 0,
+     started: false,
+     over: false
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ // The panel can be dragged while a round is running, so the sky takes the width
+ // it is given and the pipes keep the place they had in it.
+ export const widen = (game: Flappy, width: number): Flappy =>
+   width === game.width ? game : { ...game, width }
+ 
+ export function flap(game: Flappy): Flappy {
+   if (game.over) return game
+   return { ...game, started: true, vy: FLAP }
+ }
+ 
+ // The ceiling is a wall rather than a way to die. Flying off the top of the
+ // screen ends nothing in the game this is: the pipes above still catch a bird
+ // that tries to go over them, which is what it is really being kept out of.
+ const hits = (game: Flappy): boolean => {
+   if (game.y + BIRD.r >= floor) return true
+   const x = birdX(game.width)
+   return game.pipes.some(pipe => {
+     const near = x + BIRD.r > pipe.x && x - BIRD.r < pipe.x + PIPE.width
+     if (!near) return false
+     return game.y - BIRD.r < pipe.gap - PIPE.gap / 2 || game.y + BIRD.r > pipe.gap + PIPE.gap / 2
+   })
+ }
+ 
+ // One frame. The step is handed in rather than read off a clock, so a slow frame
+ // moves the world by what it was really worth and a test can step it exactly.
+ export function tick(game: Flappy, dt: number, rand: Rand = Math.random): Flappy {
+   if (game.over) return game
+   if (!game.started) return game
+   const fell = game.vy + GRAVITY * dt
+   const rose = game.y + fell * dt
+   const y = Math.max(rose, BIRD.r)
+   const vy = y > rose ? 0 : fell
+   const behind = birdX(game.width) - BIRD.r
+   const moved = game.pipes.map(pipe => ({ ...pipe, x: pipe.x - SPEED * dt }))
+   const scored = moved.filter(pipe => !pipe.passed && pipe.x + PIPE.width < behind).length
+   for (const pipe of moved) if (pipe.x + PIPE.width < behind) pipe.passed = true
+   const kept = moved.filter(pipe => pipe.x + PIPE.width > -4)
+   const last = kept[kept.length - 1]
+   const pipes =
+     last && last.x < game.width
+       ? [...kept, { x: last.x + PIPE.spacing, gap: gapAt(rand), passed: false }]
+       : kept
+   const next: Flappy = { ...game, y, vy, pipes, score: game.score + scored }
+   return hits(next) ? { ...next, over: true, y: Math.min(next.y, floor - BIRD.r) } : next
+ }
